source.title: GRIP: Algorithm-Agnostic Machine Unlearning for Mixture-of-Experts via Geometric Router Constraints
source.authors: A. Zhu; Rong-Zhe Wei; Yu-Pu Gu; Pan Li

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether unlearning leaves targeted knowledge accessible using white-box expert forcing and black-box prompt attacks, and reports the effects of a different, router-constraint method. These are conceptual tests of recovery and robustness, not the specified fine-tuning, activation-direction ablation, or quantization attacks.
record.gate_note: The paper reports attack outcomes for expert forcing, 5-shot prompting, and rephrasing. The 5-shot condition is an in-context prompt attack, not fine-tuning. The paper does not report few-example retraining, activation-direction ablation, or quantization as recovery attacks. Other unlearning and utility results are included only where they characterize the attacks or whether targeted performance was near chance with retained ability.
record.test_reason: On Qwen3-30B-A3B (WMDP-Cyber, RMU), the study measures whether forget-set knowledge returns under two kinds of attack. One is white-box Expert Forcing, which overrides the router to use the pre-unlearning experts. The other is a pair of black-box prompt attacks (5-shot and rephrase-as-poem). It compares unconstrained RMU, SEUF and its own GRIP method. This bears on A, C, E and F with a method different from the originals. It is not one of the original sources.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that standard MoE unlearning uses the router as a shortcut, hiding knowledge in experts that expert forcing partly recovers (11%, SEUF 8%). They say GRIP's hard constraints cut white-box recovery to 3%, improve retain accuracy by up to 89%, and match dense-model robustness to black-box prompt attacks. Only Method A was attacked.
record.recipe_differences: Introduces GRIP router constraints as an adapter to existing unlearning objectives; evaluates GD, KL, NPO, and RMU with training-time projection or post-training correction. It is not a reproduction of the original-source methods named in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: Attack outcome varies with unlearning method and attack: white-box Expert Forcing recovery is 11% for the unconstrained baseline, 8% for SEUF, and 3% for GRIP; black-box recovery is 11.5%, 8.5%, 4.5%, and 2.5% for the unconstrained baseline, SEUF, GRIP, and dense reference respectively. Table 8 also reports recovery varying with constraint hardness and update breadth.

fits_no_version.finding: Standard unlearning on MoE collapses retain-set routing stability (Jaccard 0.21–0.45); GRIP restores it to at least 0.94. This is a mechanism measure, not a recovery or accuracy rate.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Unlearning in MoE models achieves forgetting partly by shifting router expert selection rather than editing the experts.

record.problems: The text gives no numerical uncertainty estimates for the attack results, despite describing GRIP's 3% expert-forcing recovery as within noise margins. The white-box attack is restricted to forget queries whose routing shifted; the authors call it a worst-case diagnostic requiring full white-box access. The reported black-box suite has two prompt variants. Some ablations are explicitly single-seed.
record.rows_left_out: No results-bearing rows omitted. Other table metrics and design ablations that do not measure targeted-knowledge recovery or the near-chance/retained-ability condition were not included.

untested.parts: No relearning or fine-tuning attack of any kind.
No activation-direction ablation; only router-override expert forcing.
No quantization attack, even though unlearning was run in FP8.
Only 5-shot and rephrase-as-poem. No jailbreaks, other languages or in-context information.
GRIP was not tested against fine-tuning, quantization or jailbreaks. Method B (PTC) and the Qwen1.5-MoE model were not attack-tested. MUSE was not attack-tested.

missing.what: Unconstrained and SEUF NPO plateau at forget accuracy 0.33–0.34 and cannot reach chance. GD and KL rows (FA and RA) are also absent from the rows.
Forget accuracy depends on the null-space threshold (0.31 at 1e-4) and on the constraint formulation (0.38 with full null space).
Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B results: RMU FA 0.28 / RA 0.38; GRIP FA 0.25–0.27 / RA 0.61–0.63.
MUSE C1/C2 forget metrics and C4 utility (unconstrained utility as low as 4.31) for all four objectives.
Zero-shot MMLU and TruthfulQA retention: 86–90% and 88–89% for GRIP against about 66% and 69% for unconstrained methods.

record.verdict_notes: No uncertainty is reported for any result, yet 3% is called within noise. Pre-unlearning WMDP-Cyber accuracy is never given, so the size of recovery relative to the original model is unknown. Forced accuracy uses only routing-shifted queries while the subtracted normal FA appears to be whole-set, a possible mismatch. Table 4's caption and Appendix E define Recovery Rate differently. The Table 5 dense row may be cited rather than run. Some ablations are single-seed. Peer-reviewed at COLM 2026.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test every current unlearning method or all simple attacks; the tested attacks are expert forcing, 5-shot prompting, and rephrase-as-poem.
No fine-tuning or retraining on a small relearning set is reported.
No activation-direction ablation is reported. The paper tests a different bypass: forcing the original experts on queries whose routing shifted.
No low-bit quantization recovery test is reported.
Tests 5-shot and rephrase-as-poem prompt attacks; does not report jailbreaks, other languages, or other rephrasing types.
Tests GRIP against the reported expert-forcing and black-box prompt attacks only, not every attack named in the claim.
